issues.legal_issue: A death sentence for a premeditated multiple murder must be reduced where, after balancing the aggravating circumstances against substantial mitigating circumstances concerning the offender and the background to the crime, life imprisonment is not shown to be inadequate.
material_facts: The appeal before the Court was limited to the sentence, and the death sentence had been imposed following a murder conviction.
The offender deliberately killed multiple victims, including women and children who were asleep and had given no provocation.

The killings followed a prolonged dispute and repeated incidents of harassment and violence against the offender’s family. The offender had made repeated written requests for protection and action, but the authorities had failed to provide effective relief.
The offender was 23 years old at the time of the crime, had no previous criminal record, and was serving in a disciplined armed force.

The Court considered that the offender had felt morally justified in taking revenge, that his mental state had been affected by the continuing circumstances, and that the record gave no reason to believe he could not be reformed or would remain a continuing threat to society.
issues.conclusion: The crime, though gruesome and premeditated, was not one of the rarest of rare cases in which life imprisonment would be inadequate. The death sentence was replaced with imprisonment for life.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, death is an exceptional sentence reserved for the rarest of rare cases in which life imprisonment is inadequate. The court must balance the aggravating and mitigating circumstances, considering both the crime and the offender, and give mitigating circumstances a liberal and expansive construction. Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1980] 2 SCC 684, identifies relevant mitigating circumstances including youth, the probability of reform and rehabilitation, the offender’s belief that the act was morally justified, and mental defect affecting appreciation of the act’s criminality; the State must prove that the offender does not satisfy the relevant reformability condition. Shankar v. State of Tamil Nadu, [1994] 4 SCC 478, reiterates that death is appropriate only where the circumstances show that life imprisonment is inadequate and the offender is a menace to society.

rule.if: appeal_limited_to_sentence_after_murder_conviction and death_sentence_imposed and premeditated_multiple_killings and prolonged_family_harassment and repeated_protection_requests_went_unanswered and offender_believed_act_morally_justified and young_first_offender and no_shown_continuing_threat_or_inability_to_reform

predicates.appeal_limited_to_sentence_after_murder_: The convicted person appealed in a proceeding confined to challenging the sentence imposed after a murder conviction.
predicates.death_sentence_imposed: The court below imposed a death sentence on the convicted person.
predicates.premeditated_multiple_killings: The offender planned and carried out the killings of multiple people, including defenceless victims who were asleep.
predicates.prolonged_family_harassment: The offender’s family had experienced continuing harassment and violence connected with a dispute.
predicates.repeated_protection_requests_went_unansw: The offender repeatedly asked public authorities to protect the family and act on its complaints, but effective relief was not provided.
predicates.offender_believed_act_morally_justified: The offender believed that taking revenge was morally justified in light of the treatment of the family.
predicates.young_first_offender: The offender was young at the time of the crime and had no prior criminal record.
predicates.no_shown_continuing_threat_or_inability_: The record provided no reason to believe that the offender would continue committing violent crimes or could not be reformed.

issues.definition: When a sentence appeal after a murder conviction involves a death sentence and the listed aggravating and mitigating facts are present, the rule calls for replacing the death sentence with life imprisonment.
